strengths: Soundness: The deterministic sandwich result (Theorems 3.3/F.2) is simple but valid and useful: intersecting the synthetic-powered decision with a real-data guardrail limits worst-case risk to α+ε, while the second guardrail preserves the base procedure’s ordering-based utility. The proofs make the core mechanism transparent.

Significance: A black-box wrapper applicable to conformal prediction, risk control, single testing, and multiple testing could be practically useful, particularly because it requires little modification of existing inference procedures.

Presentation: The paper is generally readable, provides concrete interpretations of the lattice operations, and includes both simulations and diverse applications spanning proteins, LLM evaluation, anomaly detection, and vision-transformer analysis.

The experiments consistently illustrate the intended qualitative behavior: useful auxiliary data can improve power or reduce abstention, while the real-data guardrail prevents the extreme failures of synthetic-only inference.

The appendix supplies proofs, experimental details, sensitivity analyses for α, ε, sample size, and synthetic-data quality, and an impossibility result motivating why exact level-α robustness to arbitrary auxiliary data is too strong.
Research ethics: The manuscript uses established datasets and pretrained models and presents no apparent unresolved human-subject or deployment concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The practically important distribution-free guarantee is largely inherited from the real-only procedure at the relaxed level α+ε; the synthetic component can be arbitrary because it is clipped by that guardrail. The stronger quality-adaptive bounds depend on total-variation quantities that are unknown and generally inestimable, and Theorem 3.2 assumes i.i.d. synthetic observations from Q∈P. Thus the broad claim of assumption-free adaptation as synthetic quality improves is stronger than what is operationally established.

The flagship protein experiment appears to invalidate its own conformal-risk-control premise. Section B.1 defines a loss that can range up to 1 but sets the required loss bound B=0.5 merely because AlphaFold is usually accurate. Without proving or enforcing that no protein can have more than 50% high-error residues, the advertised distribution-free guarantee does not follow. Moreover, synthetic proteins are selected conditionally from MSAs of the real calibration proteins and filtered using a proxy, rather than being i.i.d. and independent as in the quality-sensitive theory.

The empirical evidence is not sufficiently rigorous for several claims. The protein study has only 38 proteins and reports 10 splits; the LLM study repeatedly subsamples a fixed 30-question benchmark; and figures mostly report distributions of repeated resampling estimates rather than uncertainty over an independently sampled target population. These designs do not convincingly validate generalization or nominal error control.

The mechanistic-interpretability Type-I-error experiment does not establish a true null: two hand-selected, disjoint groups of non-animal ImageNet classes need not have identical activation-score distributions. Similar-looking histograms cannot justify the permutation-test exchangeability null. Likewise, higher activation for selected dog classes than selected object classes is weak evidence that the head has a general animal-specific causal or functional role.

Originality is limited. Relative to the cited SPI work, the principal advance is a general lattice/Boolean formulation of clipping an arbitrary auxiliary-data procedure between two real-data procedures. This is elegant, but much of the central guarantee follows immediately from monotonicity, and the manuscript does not convincingly distinguish the construction from broader safe-testing, intersection-union, or fallback/guardrail ideas.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the experimental claims: no code or artifact availability is stated, random seeds and exact sampling conventions are missing, several preprocessing choices are underspecified, and the LLM answer audit relies on another LLM without reporting validation of that judge. Computational requirements are also absent.

Presentation contains technical inconsistencies that should be corrected, including the apparent use of Binomial(n,ρ) for each Xi in Section C.1 where Bernoulli observations seem intended, and a meet/join typo in Condition F.1. Several major figures omit readily readable numerical summaries or confidence intervals.

The limitations discussion is too narrow: it mentions only dependence of power on synthetic-data quality, omitting the α-to-α+ε validity relaxation, the unobservable quality metric, dependence and selection of synthetic samples, invalid B choice in the protein experiment, benchmark resampling limitations, and the questionable null in the vision experiment. These issues prevent the current evidence from supporting the manuscript’s broad central claims.

strengths: The core construction is simple and broadly reusable: composing a valid base procedure with lattice meet/join operations yields a deterministic sandwich between the real-data procedures at levels α and α+ε. This gives a genuine finite-sample worst-case guardrail when the base procedure and ordering assumptions are valid.

The paper explores several inference settings—conformal prediction/risk control, single and multiple testing, outlier detection, and model evaluation—and includes simulations varying synthetic-data quality, sample size, and ε.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the appendices provide formal definitions, application-specific derivations, and proofs rather than leaving the framework entirely informal.
The authors appropriately acknowledge that gains depend on synthetic-data quality; this limitation itself should not be penalized.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not isolate benefit from synthetic data at a fixed validity level. GESPI is guaranteed only at α+ε and is deterministically bounded by the real-only procedure at that relaxed level, yet experiments compare it primarily with OnlyReal at α rather than the essential Alg_{α+ε} baseline. GESPI's apparent power or abstention improvements may therefore simply reflect spending the additional ε error budget. Figure 7(d) explicitly shows its Type I error increasing approximately with α+ε.

The protein experiment invalidates its advertised conformal risk guarantee. The loss is acknowledged to be bounded by 1, but Appendix B.1 sets the conformal-risk-control bound B=0.5 based only on the empirical belief that AlphaFold is accurate. Since the loss can exceed 0.5, the prerequisite upper bound is false, so the reported distribution-free guarantee does not apply.

The theoretical novelty is limited. The main unconditional result is essentially the immediate monotonicity observation that intersecting/AND-ing with a valid α+ε procedure cannot have larger loss, while union/OR with the α procedure prevents worse utility than that baseline. The distribution-sensitive bounds use total-variation distances between induced loss distributions that are unknown and generally not estimable from the available data, limiting their operational value.

Several claims overstate what is established. In particular, the discussion says GESPI 'never underperforms' while its validity can be worse by ε; the experiments repeatedly describe control near nominal α although the theorem permits α+ε; and rejection frequency on a fixed, resampled 30-question AIME dataset is called statistical power without defining a population-level alternative or providing uncertainty for the asserted model ranking.

The mechanistic-interpretability Type I-error experiment does not establish a null setting: two disjoint mixtures of non-animal ImageNet classes need not have identical activation-score distributions, and visual similarity of histograms is not proof of the exchangeability required by the permutation test. There is also a concrete specification inconsistency: L22H6 is described as 'layer 6, head 22' in Figure 15, even though the stated architecture has only 16 heads.

The empirical evidence is difficult to audit. Most results are small plots without numerical tables or confidence intervals, some experiments use only 10 repetitions, and no code or reproducibility artifact is identified. Exact random seeds, sampled splits, generated data, and several implementation choices are unavailable; the LLM section also mixes figure labels indicating temperature 0 with default generation details specifying temperature 0.6.

There are technical and presentation defects in the appendix: Condition F.1 contains an apparent meet/join typo, the proof of Theorem H.3 writes total variation where Pinsker's inequality requires KL divergence, and Proposition E.1's displayed inequalities do not justify the accompanying claim that a real-only method dominates the synthetic-data method in utility.

The limitations discussion is too narrow. It mentions dependence on synthetic-data quality but omits the relaxed α+ε validity target, the missing equal-validity baseline, the invalid B=0.5 assumption, computational costs of AlphaFold/LLM/FLUX generation, and risks from model-based answer grading. No substantive research-ethics or broader-impact discussion is provided, although no acute ethical violation is apparent from the described studies.

strengths: Soundness: The central guardrail construction is simple and largely convincing. Under the stated bounded-loss, lattice, monotonicity, and nesting conditions, Theorems 3.2–3.3 show finite-sample risk at most α+ε for arbitrary synthetic-data quality, while the two-sided version is deterministically sandwiched between the real-only procedures at α and α+ε.

Significance: A black-box wrapper applicable to conformal prediction/risk control, one- and multiple-hypothesis testing, and related inference problems is potentially useful. It offers a practical way to exploit auxiliary data without fully trusting its distribution.

Originality: The work provides a meaningful generalization and decision-theoretic interpretation of synthetic-powered predictive inference, extending the basic guardrail idea beyond conformal prediction rather than merely proposing another task-specific estimator.

Evaluation: The paper includes simulations, AlphaFold protein experiments, AIME/OlympiadBench model comparisons, three outlier benchmarks, and a vision-transformer interpretability study. The synthetic-quality, ε, α, n, and N ablations help expose when gains arise and when the guardrail activates.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally clear and includes substantial implementation detail, including datasets, sample sizes, model checkpoints, prompts, test constructions, hyperparameters, and repetition counts. The proofs are supplied, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent from the use of public datasets and models.
weaknesses: Soundness: The AlphaFold experiment does not retain the advertised distribution-free guarantee. The residue-level loss is explicitly bounded by 1, but Appendix B.1 sets the conformal-risk-control bound to B=0.5 merely because AlphaFold is empirically accurate. Unless it is proven that every possible test protein has loss at most 0.5, the base conformal guarantee—and consequently GESPI's guarantee for this flagship application—does not follow.

Soundness: The multiple-outlier experiment uses the Simes–Hochberg procedure, whose FWER validity generally needs independence or suitable positive dependence. The manuscript does not establish these conditions for conformal p-values sharing a reference set, so the required validity of the base algorithm is unclear.

Claims and significance: GESPI can improve utility only within the range between the real-only procedures at α and α+ε. Thus part of the apparent gain is purchased by allowing additional error ε, and comparison against real-only at α+ε is missing. This baseline is essential for determining how much benefit is genuinely attributable to synthetic data.

Originality/scope: The method is an elegant but elementary lattice clipping/aggregation construction closely inspired by prior SPI. It does not literally wrap any inference procedure: it requires a bounded monotone loss, a distributive lattice of actions, and procedures nested in α. The abstract and discussion understate these restrictions.

Evaluation: Several empirical studies use very small underlying datasets—38 proteins and 30 AIME25 questions—with repeated resampling of the same finite collection. These rejection frequencies should not be interpreted straightforwardly as population power or Type-I error, and numerical tables or uncertainty intervals are largely absent.

Theory: Proposition E.1 states that a real-only algorithm dominates the synthetic procedure, but its proof only obtains domination up to an additive δ when the relevant supremum need not be attained. There are also definition/proof typographical errors in Condition F.1 and the Pinsker step of Theorem H.3. These appear repairable but weaken confidence in the theoretical presentation.

Reproducibility and limitations: No code, random seeds, exact sampled splits, or artifact link is provided. The limitations section mentions only dependence on synthetic-data quality and omits the α+ε tradeoff, the structural assumptions, the invalid B=0.5 choice, and dependence requirements of the base procedures. Ethical risk is low, but dataset/model licensing and computational cost are not discussed.

strengths: The central GESPI construction is simple, general, and practically implementable: lattice-style aggregation sandwiches the synthetic-powered action between procedures using real data at levels α and α+ε. This yields a clear finite-sample worst-case guarantee at α+ε regardless of synthetic-data quality and deterministic utility dominance over the α-level base action under the stated ordering assumptions.

The paper gives a useful unifying decision-theoretic treatment spanning conformal prediction, conformal risk control, single and multiple hypothesis testing, and confidence sets. The main sandwich result is broadly applicable, including when the synthetic-powered component is data-dependent.

The manuscript is generally well organized and intuitive. It clearly explains the role of ε as an admission cost and distinguishes the guaranteed GESPI procedure from unsafe OnlySynth and pooled-data baselines.

The evaluation is unusually broad, including simulations, ImageNet/FLUX conformal prediction, protein structure prediction, outlier detection, LLM comparison, and mechanistic interpretability. Several experiments vary synthetic quality, sample size, α, and ε, and full-result appendices are provided.

The work has meaningful, though modest, originality: its main contribution is not a new base inference method but a general black-box guardrail construction and a common perspective connecting several inference tasks.
weaknesses: The strongest guarantee is control at α+ε, not at the nominal target α. The deterministic utility improvement over the α-level baseline is therefore partly purchased by permitting additional error, while the α+ε real-only guardrail always has at least as much ordered utility as GESPI. The paper explains this tradeoff but occasionally overstates the result as error control at the desired or nominal level.

The claimed adaptation toward α is substantially weaker than the headline suggests. The general two-sided result contains an additional τ term even when P=Q, and the total-variation notion of synthetic quality is procedure-dependent, generally unobservable, and difficult to interpret or verify. The text also incorrectly discusses this TV distance as tending to infinity even though TV is bounded.

The flagship protein risk-control experiment does not support its advertised distribution-free guarantee. The loss is a fraction and can be as large as 1, but Appendix B.2 sets the conformal-risk-control bound B=0.5 merely because AlphaFold is empirically accurate. B must be a valid upper bound, not a typical observed value. This is especially consequential for n=10 and α=0.05: using the valid bound B=1 makes the minimum correction 1/11, so the reported nontrivial 5% result would not be certified.

Some empirical validity checks do not instantiate a known null. In the mechanistic-interpretability experiment, two disjoint sets of non-animal ImageNet classes are asserted to have equal activation-score distributions based on similar histograms; that equality is not guaranteed, so the reported rejection frequency is not a Type-I-error estimate. Likewise, the LLM study repeatedly resamples from only 30 AIME problems and applies an i.i.d. binomial model without adequately addressing finite-population sampling, question heterogeneity, or dependence from reused generations.

Several showcased comparisons are explicitly oracle or retrospective: ROC curves match methods using empirical error, and the equal-coverage conformal comparison aligns methods using test coverage unavailable in practice. These are informative diagnostics but provide limited evidence for deployable gains. Statistical uncertainty is also incompletely reported despite small datasets and nested repetitions.

There are proof-presentation issues that require correction. In the proof of Theorem F.2, the displayed lower-bound derivation is circular as written; it needs to substitute the pooled action on event E. The subsequent TV comparison also retains V distributed as T(P) while invoking a distance whose second distribution is defined using T(Q). Both appear repairable, but the current proof does not formally establish the stated result.

Reproducibility is only partial. The appendix provides many model, dataset, and sampling details, but the manuscript’s software link is blank, and seeds, exact environment/package versions, generated artifacts, computational cost, and some data-filtering choices are missing. The AlphaFold synthetic construction also depends on real-data-derived MSAs, so it does not satisfy the independent i.i.d. P/Q setup used by the quality-dependent theory, although the worst-case sandwich guarantee itself is more robust.

The limitations discussion is too narrow, mentioning only dependence of power on synthetic quality. It should also acknowledge that gains require an α-to-α+ε relaxation, that useful synthetic data are not guaranteed, that the quality bounds are not operational, and that several experiments rely on questionable modeling or calibration assumptions. No dedicated ethics or broader-impact discussion is included; no severe ethical issue is apparent, but data/model licensing and substantial generation/compute costs should be documented.

strengths: The lattice-based wrapper is simple, broadly applicable, and its core sandwich guarantee is easy to understand: the two-sided construction lies pointwise between the real-only procedures at levels α and α+ε.

The paper explores an unusually broad collection of applications, including conformal prediction, hypothesis testing, multiple testing, protein structure prediction, and LLM evaluation, together with simulations and several ablations.
The manuscript is generally organized well, and the appendices provide formal definitions, proofs, and substantial experimental detail.

The work recognizes that synthetic data may be arbitrarily unreliable and does not claim that naïvely pooling such data preserves validity. No major research-ethics concern is apparent from the reported use of public datasets and models.
weaknesses: The central guarantee is substantially weaker than the framing suggests. GESPI controls worst-case risk only at α+ε, not at the desired level α; this follows almost immediately because the output is bounded by the real-only α+ε procedure. The method therefore purchases its gains by relaxing the error guarantee. Experiments do not convincingly separate benefits attributable to synthetic data from benefits attributable to this relaxation.

The claim that GESPI 'defaults to the standard method' when synthetic data are poor is inaccurate. Adverse synthetic data can push the two-sided procedure anywhere up to the α+ε guardrail, increasing error relative to the α-level base method. Likewise, the TV bounds do not establish that realized error monotonically decreases as synthetic quality improves. The relevant distances are also unobservable and algorithm-dependent.

The flagship AlphaFold experiment does not instantiate the stated conformal-risk-control assumptions. Its loss is a fraction and therefore has deterministic upper bound 1, yet the authors set the CRC bound B=0.5 merely because AlphaFold is empirically accurate. Unless every possible protein is guaranteed to have loss at most 0.5, the claimed distribution-free risk guarantee does not follow.

The empirical comparisons often favor the α+ε Guardrail in utility; for example, the ImageNet tables show smaller sets for Guardrail than for GESPI. GESPI is instead justified through lower variability or risk closer to α, but those properties are not consequences of the principal sandwich theorem. Fair comparisons against alternative real-only procedures calibrated to the same achieved error, including randomized/interpolated tests, are missing.

The stated impossibility result does not justify its interpretation. Proposition E.1 compares worst-case risks and constructs a real-only procedure whose risk is at least the synthetic procedure's worst-case risk up to δ; it neither proves pointwise domination nor establishes higher power, narrower sets, or impossibility of useful synthetic-data-assisted procedures under level-α control. The surrounding claims therefore overreach the proposition.

Some validation protocols are questionable. In the mechanistic-interpretability experiment, two groups of different non-animal classes are merely 'expected' to have equal activation distributions; this does not create a genuine null, so the resulting rejection frequency is not a valid Type-I-error estimate. For multiple outlier testing, the assumptions under which the shared-reference conformal p-values and the chosen Hochberg procedure control FWER are not clearly established.

The genericity claim is overstated: the wrapper requires a distributive lattice, monotonicity in α, bounded monotone loss, and compatible nested outputs, so it does not wrap 'any' inference procedure. Theorem 3.4 supplies an ordering, not a general utility guarantee without an additional utility-order relationship.

Presentation contains consequential imprecision: the text discusses a total-variation distance tending to infinity even though TV is bounded by one, figures are often too small to read comfortably, and the limitations section mentions only dependence on synthetic-data quality while omitting the α+ε tradeoff, unverifiable quality distances, and application-specific assumption failures.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance. The software footnote has a blank URL, random seeds and exact sampled splits are not supplied, and several experiments depend on expensive generated artifacts or model outputs that are not provided. The paper also lacks a substantive discussion of dataset/model licensing, benchmark contamination, or biases in generated data, although these do not appear to create an immediate severe ethical risk.

strengths: Soundness: The central guardrail construction is mathematically clean. Under the stated lattice, nesting, bounded-loss, and monotonicity assumptions, clipping the synthetic-powered action between real-only actions at levels α and α+ε directly yields finite-sample, distribution-free worst-case control. The proofs are generally transparent and consistent with the claims.

Significance: A black-box wrapper applicable to conformal prediction, risk control, single and multiple testing could be practically useful when auxiliary data are plentiful but unreliable. The deterministic guarantee that the two-sided procedure is no less useful than the α-level base action and no more aggressive than the α+ε action is especially interpretable.

Evaluation: The paper covers unusually diverse applications, including ImageNet/FLUX, AlphaFold/CASP-14, conformal outlier detection, mathematical-reasoning model comparisons, and a vision-transformer case study. Simulations appropriately examine synthetic-data quality, n, N, α, and ε; the comparison with SPI also helps position the conformal-prediction contribution.

Originality: Although the underlying clipping operation is simple, casting it as a general decision-theoretic mechanism and working out its use across several inference problems provides a useful new synthesis beyond the prior conformal-specific SPI method.

Presentation and reproducibility: The exposition is clear, intuitive examples accompany the abstraction, proofs and substantial experimental details are included, and most datasets, models, hyperparameters, trial counts, and base procedures are identified.
weaknesses: The main guarantee controls error only at α+ε for arbitrary synthetic data, rather than at the nominal α. Thus the strongest distribution-free protection comes entirely from the more permissive real-only guardrail. Many gains approach those of Guardrail, making it difficult to determine how much benefit comes from synthetic data rather than spending the additional error budget. The paper should more consistently qualify claims of “error-rate control” and compare against real-only procedures calibrated to matched empirical error or utility.

The claimed applicability to “any” or essentially any base inference method is overstated. Condition F.1 requires a distributive lattice, bounded monotone loss, and pointwise nesting of the base algorithm in α. These are substantive restrictions that many non-nested tests, confidence regions, randomized procedures, and multidimensional actions do not satisfy. Moreover, the deterministic order sandwich represents utility only where that order genuinely captures the application’s utility.

The general synthetic-quality quantity is a total-variation distance between induced loss distributions. It depends on the unknown target distribution and the chosen algorithm, is not estimable in the presented setting, and can be nearly as difficult to characterize as the original risk. Consequently, the advertised gradual adaptation-to-quality guarantee is often qualitative or vacuous outside the specialized conformal and median examples.

The headline AlphaFold experiment does not retain the stated conformal risk-control guarantee: the residue-level loss is bounded by 1, but the conformal correction uses B=0.5 merely because AlphaFold is empirically accurate. This is not a valid distribution-free upper bound on the loss. Combined with only 38 proteins, n=10 calibration proteins, 10 repetitions, and substantial data-dependent construction of synthetic proteins, this application is suggestive rather than convincing evidence of reliable risk control.

Several evaluations are weaker than their breadth suggests. Most baselines are either the real-only method, the α+ε guardrail, or knowingly invalid pooling; competitive robust/auxiliary-data methods are largely absent. Some ROC and matched-coverage comparisons use oracle knowledge unavailable in practice. The mechanistic-interpretability study confirms a previously selected head on hand-selected classes, while the LLM study uses only 30 AIME questions and an LLM-based fallback judge without a reported manual error audit.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite extensive procedural detail: the manuscript’s software link is blank, exact sampled subsets and random seeds are not supplied, and some claimed per-class counts are missing. Reproducing the FLUX, AlphaFold, and 32k-token majority-vote experiments would also require substantial unquantified compute.

Limitations and ethics receive little treatment. The discussion mentions only dependence on synthetic-data quality, omitting the α-to-α+ε validity tradeoff, restrictive structural assumptions, invalid B=0.5 choice in the protein experiment, benchmark-selection effects, and evaluator bias. There are no major apparent ethical violations, but downstream biomedical interpretation and the environmental/computational cost of the large generation workloads deserve explicit discussion.
